title: Living Stones and Christ's Example
summary: Peter calls believers to put away malice and grow like newborns craving milk. Coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, they are being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, and they are now God's chosen people, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation. As foreigners and exiles they are to live honorably among unbelievers, respect human authorities, and, as household servants, endure unjust suffering after the example of Christ, who bore our sins on the tree.
story: Chapter 1 told the readers that God had given them new birth through his enduring word. Chapter 2 tells them what they have been born into: a people, a house, a priesthood. The chapter gathers titles and promises that belonged to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5-6) and in the prophets (Isaiah 28:16; Hosea 1-2) and gives them to a church of mostly Gentile believers. It then turns outward, beginning the letter's long section on how God's people should live among those who do not share their faith. Its closing verses, drawn from Isaiah 53, are among the New Testament's most important statements about the meaning of Christ's death.
historical:
Verse 13 speaks of “the king as the supreme authority” and of governors sent by him. In the eastern Roman Empire the emperor was commonly called king (basileus), and the provinces were administered by governors who kept order and administered justice. If Peter wrote in the early 60s AD, the emperor was Nero. Peter's instruction to honor him is not approval of everything a ruler does; it is a principle for Christian citizenship that stops short of worship, since the same verse reserves fear for God alone.

The servants of verse 18 are household slaves (oiketai). Slavery was built into the economy and household structure of the Roman world, and slaves were a substantial part of the population in many regions. Household slaves worked as cooks, cleaners, tutors, stewards, and secretaries. Their treatment depended heavily on the master; they had few legal protections and could be beaten. Many early converts were slaves, and Peter addresses them directly as members of the church and as people responsible before God, something ancient household instructions rarely did.
cultural:
Stones and buildings were a familiar language for God's dwelling. The Jerusalem temple, still standing if the letter dates before AD 70, was the house of God and the place of priests and sacrifice. Peter says God is now building a different house out of living stones, the believers, with Christ as its cornerstone, the foundation stone that set the line for the whole building. The Old Testament texts he cites (Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 8:14) were already read together by early Christians as a set of stone prophecies about Jesus.

The Gentile neighbors who slandered the readers as evildoers (verse 12) likely saw them as antisocial. Christians refused to join in civic festivals honoring the gods, avoided temple banquets, and met privately, and rumors about their meetings circulated. Peter's answer is that good deeds, visible over time, can overturn slander. The phrase “the day He visits us” draws on an Old Testament expression for God's coming in mercy or judgment.
literary: The chapter moves from identity to conduct. Verses 1-3 continue the call of chapter 1 with the image of newborns and milk. Verses 4-10 form a dense cluster of Old Testament citations and allusions built around the catchword stone, which is then followed by the great titles of verse 9 (drawn from Exodus 19:6 and Isaiah 43:20-21) and the reversal of Hosea's names in verse 10 (“not a people” becoming “the people of God”). Verse 11 opens a new section with “Beloved, I urge you”, which runs to 4:11. Verses 13-25 begin a household code, a form of ancient moral instruction arranging duties within society and family, which continues into chapter 3. The section on servants climaxes in a poetic passage about Christ (verses 21-25) that weaves together phrases from Isaiah 53:4-12.

outline.t: The living stone and the living stones
A chosen people and a royal priesthood
Christ's example and his sin-bearing death

doctrines.note: The church is “a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession.” Every believer shares in this priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices, and the church exists to proclaim the virtues of the God who called it out of darkness.

“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.” Christ's death is substitutionary (he bore our sins) and transforming (we die to sin and are healed).

Suffering unjustly while doing good, and entrusting oneself to God, is commendable before God because it follows the path Christ walked. Peter does not call injustice good; he calls faithful endurance of it good.
Believers' good conduct among unbelievers is a form of witness, so that slanderers “may see your good deeds and glorify God.” The church's calling is to proclaim God's virtues in word and life.

words.note: Lithos, stone. Peter uses it five times in the chapter. Christ is the living stone, rejected by builders but chosen by God, and believers become living stones in God's house. For those who believe the stone is precious; for those who refuse, it becomes a stone they trip over. The image joins Christ and his people in one building.

Hierateuma, priesthood or a body of priests, drawn from Exodus 19:6 in the Greek Old Testament. In Israel only the descendants of Aaron served as priests. Peter gives the title to the whole church, offering spiritual sacrifices, the root of the later teaching often called the priesthood of all believers.

Paroikos, a resident alien or foreigner, someone living in a place without citizenship. Paired with parepidēmos (exile), it describes believers as people whose true belonging is elsewhere, like Abraham in Canaan (Genesis 23:4), and whose life among others must therefore be especially careful and honorable.

Hupogrammos, example. The word described a model of letters that a child traced over or copied when learning to write. Christ's suffering is the pattern believers trace, following “in His footsteps”. It appears only here in the New Testament.

christ: Christ is the living stone and the cornerstone, the fulfillment of the stone prophecies of Isaiah and the Psalms: rejected by people, chosen and precious to God, and the foundation of a new temple made of people. In verses 21-25 Peter, who once tried to talk Jesus out of the cross (Mark 8:31-33), presents Christ's suffering in the words of Isaiah 53: he committed no sin, no deceit was in his mouth, he did not retaliate, he entrusted himself to God, he bore our sins, and by his wounds we are healed. Christ is both example and substitute: believers follow his steps in suffering, but only he could bear their sins. The chapter ends by calling him “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls”, recalling Jesus' own words that he is the good shepherd (John 10:11) and Peter's commission to feed his sheep (John 21:15-17).

hard.q: Does Peter's instruction to servants endorse slavery or require victims to accept abuse?
hard.a:
Peter addresses household slaves in a society where slavery was universal and where Christians had no political power to abolish it. He does not defend slavery as an institution, but he also does not call for its abolition, and readers are right to feel the weight of that. Several points help. First, Peter treats slaves as full members of the church and moral agents answerable to God, something the household codes of his culture rarely did. Second, he grounds their conduct not in the master's rights but in Christ's example, and he calls unjust treatment what it is: unjust. Third, the principles of the New Testament (all people made in God's image, masters and slaves equal before Christ, Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16) eventually led many Christians to fight slavery, although other Christians defended it, a history the church must remember honestly.

This passage speaks to people with no way out who must decide how to respond to mistreatment. It does not require anyone who can escape abuse to remain in it. Paul told slaves who could gain their freedom to take it (1 Corinthians 7:21). Anyone experiencing abuse at home, at work, or in a church should seek safety and help from trusted people, pastors, counselors, or the authorities.

questions: Peter gives a mostly Gentile church titles that once belonged to Israel. What does it mean for your sense of identity to be part of “a chosen people, a royal priesthood”?
How can good deeds overturn slander in your setting? Where have you seen that happen?
Christ is both the example we follow and the substitute who bore our sins. Why is it important to hold both together?
